name: Brushing technique (boar bristle)

lead: A boar bristle brush uses natural bristles that are tightly spaced to smooth hair. Fans say it spreads scalp oil and adds shine.
Reference sources describe the smoothing design but do not report oil-distribution effects.

paras: Tight bristles create tension that smooths strands. Proponents add that brushing carries natural oil down the shaft; this has not been tested in published studies.
Hairbrush references list no specific hazards. Designs such as cushion and detangler brushes are intended to reduce breakage [1].

lead: Boar bristle brushing means using a brush with natural boar hair bristles to smooth and style hair. Such brushes are described as having tightly spaced bristles that increase tension while brushing in order to smooth the hair [1].

Hair-care communities often say brushing spreads scalp oil along the hair and adds shine. Reference sources on hairbrushes do not make claims about oil distribution, and no clinical studies of this effect were found [1].
infobox: Boar, horsehair, nylon, stainless steel, goat [1]

paras: Hairbrushes include round, vent, cushion, paddle and detangler designs, and bristles may be boar, horsehair, nylon, steel or goat hair; handles are made from woods or plastics [1]. Cushion, paddle and detangler designs are intended to reduce breakage during detangling [1].
An 1854 US patent granted to Hugh Rock is cited as the earliest for a modern hairbrush; later patents include Samuel Firey in 1870 and Lyda D. Newman in 1898 [1].

Conditioning products are described as working by reducing friction between strands so hair combs more smoothly [2]. An undamaged cuticle is coated with a lipid film that lowers friction, and weathering, bleaching and heat styling can strip it [2]. Proponents of boar bristle brushing say the brush moves natural oils from scalp to ends, but reference sources do not report this [1].
Brushing is discussed alongside hair-care routines for smoothness and shine. A general hairstyling reference describes the old "100 strokes a day" rule as outdated [3].

timeline.event: Hugh Rock receives the earliest US patent for a modern hairbrush. [1]
Samuel Firey patents a brush with wire teeth and natural bristles. [1]
Lyda D. Newman patents an improved hairbrush. [1]
